name: Andvaranaut
powers: Cursed to bring death and misfortune to every possessor after the dwarf who made it.
description: The ring at the heart of the treasure of the dwarf Andvari, which Loki took from him under the island of the waterfall after catching him in the shape of a pike. Andvari cursed the ring and all the gold, so that it would destroy whoever possessed it. The treasure passed to Hreiðmarr, to the dragon Fáfnir, then to Sigurðr, and brought ruin upon each — a story retold in the Völsunga saga and echoed in the Nibelungenlied.

name: Ægishjálmr
powers: Strikes fear into enemies and grants the wearer protection in battle.
description: The Helm of Awe, an Icelandic magical stave drawn as a cross with branching prongs. In the Eddas it is the treasure of Fáfnir the dragon, which made its bearer invincible; in later Icelandic grimoires (galdrabækur) it was drawn on the forehead between the brows to terrify opponents and grant victory. Modern folk practice still reproduces it as a protective sign.

name: Amber Jewelry
description: Necklaces, pendants, and beads of Baltic amber, the fossil resin thrown up on Danish shores, worn as adornment and as protection since the Stone Age. Danish Bronze Age graves hold hundreds of amber beads, and amber amulets were believed to guard against the evil eye and sickness. In the Baltic legend the sea-goddess Juratė's palace of amber broke apart and scattered the amber across the waves.
source: Bronze Age graves, Denmark; Baltic amber legend

name: Aegis
powers: Scatters armies with terror; bears the head of Medusa (gorgoneion).
description: The storm-bearing shield of Zeus, lent to Athena and sometimes Apollo, an aegis of goatskin fringed with gold tassels; in Homer it scatters armies and houses the gorgoneion, the severed head of Medusa. Hephaestus forged its golden version for Zeus. It marks divine protection and terror in Greek epic.
source: Homer, Iliad (with the gorgoneion also in Hesiod and later mythographers)

name: Shield of Achilles
material: Bronze, tin, gold, silver with enamelled core
powers: Depicts the whole cosmos: earth, sea, sky, two cities, war, peace, and the encircling Ocean; impenetrable in battle.
description: The shield Hephaestus forged for Achilles, described at length in the Iliad: a five-layered shield with scenes of earth, sea, sky, sun, moon, two cities, a lawsuit, war, farming, harvest, and dance, all framed by Ocean. It is the archetype of the crafted cosmic artifact in Greek epic.

name: Crown of Ariadne
powers: Set among the stars as the constellation Corona Borealis after Ariadne's death.
description: The golden crown Ariadne wore when Theseus rescued her from Crete; Dionysus later set it in the heavens as the constellation Corona Borealis. Catullus and later poets tell how the crown commemorates the abandoned bride of Naxos, transformed into a circlet of stars.

name: Shield of Aeneas
powers: Shows the future of Rome, from Romulus to the triumph of Augustus at Actium.
description: The shield Vulcan forged for Aeneas, engraved with the future of Rome: Romulus and Remus, the rape of the Sabines, and the triumph of Augustus at Actium. Virgil describes it at the close of Aeneid 8 as the destiny of the Trojan line made visible in bronze.

name: Ancile
maker: Fell from heaven in the reign of Numa; copies made by the smith Mamurius Veturius
powers: Pledge of Rome's eternity; twelve copies kept the true shield hidden from thieves.
description: The sacred shield of Mars that fell from heaven in the reign of Numa, taken as a pledge of Rome's eternity; Numa had eleven identical copies made so that thieves could not identify it, and the Salii guarded and carried all twelve in the March procession. Plutarch, Ovid, and Servius tell the legend.
source: Plutarch, Life of Numa; Ovid, Fasti (Book 3); Servius, on the Aeneid

name: Aegis
powers: Provides impenetrable protection and bears the terrifying visage of Medusa.
description: The Aegis is Zeus's shield, forged by Hephaestus, famed for its protective power and fearsome appearance.

name: Ankh
powers: Symbol of life; grants vitality to the bearer.
description: The ankh is a looped cross symbol widely used in ancient Egyptian art, representing the concept of eternal life. It appears in tomb paintings and temple reliefs held by deities and pharaohs alike, signifying their divine right to live forever.

name: Sword of Attila
material: Iron with gold and gem-set hilt
powers: Blade of world dominion pledged to Attila.
description: The sword said to have belonged to Attila the Hun and kept among Hungarian royal treasures. The Roman historian Jordanes records that a shepherd found a blade in the ground that Attila called the Sword of Mars, pledge of world dominion. The gilded iron saber shown in Vienna's Kunsthistorisches Museum is identified with it in later tradition.

name: Arthur's Mantle
powers: Made the wearer invisible while still allowing them to see everything around them.
description: Arthur's mantle, one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain. Whoever wore it became invisible, though the wearer could still see everything about them. The mantle belongs to the Arthur of the medieval Welsh marvel-list tradition, distinct from the later continental Arthur of Malory, and is recorded only in the Welsh treasure catalogue.
source: Medieval Welsh list of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain

name: Ardagh Chalice
material: Silver, bronze, gold filigree, glass and enamel
description: The Ardagh Chalice, a silver-and-bronze liturgical cup made around the eighth century, found in 1868 in a ring-fort at Ardagh, County Limerick, with a hoard of other church metalwork. Its decorated panels of gold filigree, glass and enamel mark it as a masterpiece of Insular art; it is held by the National Museum of Ireland.

name: The Arrow of Arash
powers: Its single flight fixed the boundary between Iran and Turan.
description: The arrow shot by Arash the archer from the summit of Mount Damavand to fix the frontier between Iran and Turan, a flight blessed in the myth by the giving of his own strength, covering hundreds of miles before falling on the far bank of the Oxus. Ferdowsi and earlier Persian sources recount how Arash was chosen for the feat, and modern poetry revived the story as a symbol of national sacrifice.

name: Aladdin's Lamp
powers: Rubbed, it summoned a powerful jinni who granted its holder's wishes.
description: The lamp of the tale of Aladdin, added to the Thousand and One Nights by Antoine Galland from the Syrian storyteller Hanna Diyab around 1709. Rubbing it summoned a powerful jinni who granted wishes, while its twin, the magician's lamp, drove the plot's theft and recovery. No medieval Arabic original of the tale survives, so the lamp is a literary invention of the folk tradition.

name: The Ark of the Covenant
powers: Carried before Israel and kept in the Holy of Holies as the throne of God's presence.
description: The gilded chest built at Sinai to hold the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments, carried before the Israelites and kept in the Holy of Holies of the Jerusalem Temple. Legend holds it was hidden before the Babylonian destruction, while Ethiopian tradition claims it rests at Aksum. Its descriptions come from the biblical books; no archaeological witness survives.

name: Atlatl
material: Carved wood with antler or bone spur
powers: Hurls a dart with far greater force than an unaided arm.
description: A carved wooden device that hurls darts with far greater force than an unaided arm, used across Mesoamerica from the Olmec era to the Aztec empire. Spanish accounts and Aztec codices show warriors and hunters gripping the notched end while the dart rests in its socket, and its power is credited with punching through metal armor at short range.
source: Florentine Codex and early Spanish accounts

name: Aztec Death Whistle
powers: Cuts through battle with a terrifying shriek.
description: A small clay whistle shaped like a skull that produces a piercing, shrieking tone, first widely publicized after a skeleton-like example was found at the Templo Mayor. Whether such whistles served in battle, ritual or mourning is debated, though many plain and figure-shaped examples are documented in Aztec collections. The disturbing sound has made it famous in museum displays and recordings.
source: Templo Mayor excavations and museum collections

name: Asson
material: Gourd rattle with snake vertebrae and beads
era: Haitian Vodou tradition to the present
powers: Rings the spirits into the peristyle at ceremony.
description: The rattle of Haitian Vodou, a gourd fitted with a handle and strung with snake vertebrae and beads, shaken by the houngan or mambo to summon the lwa into the peristyle (temple) at ceremonies. Only the priest or priestess handles it, and its shaking marks the moment the spirits arrive to possess the faithful. The asson is among the most sacred objects of Vodou ritual.
source: Haitian Vodou practice and ethnographic studies

name: Amauti
material: Caribou skin with a large back hood
powers: Carries a baby in warmth against its mother's back.
description: The woman's parka of the Inuit, cut with a large hood and a deep pouch across the back in which a baby rides warm against its mother's skin; the amauti is sewn of caribou skin by the women, who are famed for the accuracy of their cutting and stitching. The pouch lets the child nurse and sleep without being taken out into the cold. It is one of the most admired garments of the Arctic.
source: Inuit tradition and Arctic ethnographic records
